title: Hwæt! Wē Gār-Dena
source: Beowulf 1–11 (text of ASPR IV, ed. Dobbie; macrons and hyphens added)
about: The opening of Beowulf, the longest poem in Old English. Before we meet the hero, the poet calls for attention and tells of Scyld Scefing, the foundling who became king of the Danes.

badge.name: Spear-Dane
badge.about: Read the opening lines of Beowulf

lines.t: Hwæt! Wē Gār-Dena in gēar-dagum,
lines.en: Listen! We have heard of the Spear-Danes in days of old,

q.prompt: Which people does the poem begin with?

lines.t: þēod-cyninga, þrym gefrūnon,
lines.en: the glory of the people's kings,

lines.t: hū ðā æþelingas ellen fremedon.
lines.en: how those princes did deeds of courage.

q.prompt: What did the princes do?

lines.t: Oft Scyld Scēfing sceaþena þrēatum, monegum mǣgþum, meodo-setla oftēah,
lines.en: Often Scyld Scefing took the mead-benches away from troops of enemies, from many tribes,

lines.t: egsode eorlas.
lines.en: and terrified warriors.

q.prompt: What did Scyld do to his enemies?
options: he took their mead-benches and terrified them

lines.t: Syððan ǣrest wearð fēa-sceaft funden, hē þæs frōfre gebād,
lines.en: After he was first found destitute, he lived to see comfort for that:

q.prompt: How did Scyld's life begin?
options: he was found alone and destitute
he was born a king's son

lines.t: wēox under wolcnum, weorð-myndum þāh,
lines.en: he grew under the skies and prospered in honours,

lines.t: oðþæt him ǣghwylc þāra ymb-sittendra ofer hron-rāde hȳran scolde,
lines.en: until each of the neighbouring peoples across the whale-road had to obey him

q.prompt: What is the 'whale-road'?

lines.t: gomban gyldan.
lines.en: and pay tribute.

lines.t: Þæt wæs gōd cyning!
lines.en: That was a good king!

q.prompt: What does the poet think of Scyld?
options: he was no king at all

title: Fæder ūre
source: The Lord's Prayer, West Saxon Gospels, Matthew 6:9–13 (c. 1000; ed. Thorpe, macrons added)
about: The Lord's Prayer as it was read in English churches around the year 1000, from the first complete translation of the Gospels into English.

badge.name: Paternoster
badge.about: Read the Lord's Prayer in Old English

lines.t: Fæder ūre þū þe eart on heofonum,
lines.en: Our Father, you who are in heaven,

q.prompt: Where is the Father?

lines.t: sī þīn nama gehālgod.
lines.en: may your name be hallowed.

lines.t: Tō becume þīn rīce,
lines.en: May your kingdom come,

lines.t: gewurþe ðīn willa, on eorðan swā swā on heofonum.
lines.en: may your will be done, on earth as in heaven.

q.prompt: Where should God's will be done?

lines.t: Ūrne gedæghwāmlīcan hlāf syle ūs tōdæg,
lines.en: Give us today our daily bread,

lines.t: and forgyf ūs ūre gyltas,
lines.en: and forgive us our sins,

lines.t: swā swā wē forgyfað ūrum gyltendum.
lines.en: just as we forgive those who sin against us.

q.prompt: Whom do we forgive?

lines.t: And ne gelǣd þū ūs on costnunge,
lines.en: And do not lead us into temptation,

lines.t: ac ālȳs ūs of yfele.
lines.en: but free us from evil.

q.prompt: What does the prayer ask to be freed from?

lines.t: Sōþlīce.
lines.en: Truly. (Amen.)

title: Cædmon's Hymn
source: Cædmon's Hymn, West Saxon eorðan version from the Old English Bede (critical text ed. O'Donnell; macrons added)
about: Bede tells of Cædmon, a cowherd at Whitby who could not sing, until a figure in a dream told him to sing of the Creation. These nine lines are what he sang, the oldest English poem by a named poet.

badge.name: Cowherd's Song
badge.about: Read Cædmon's Hymn, the first named English poem

lines.t: Nū sculon herigean heofonrīces weard,
lines.en: Now we must praise the guardian of heaven's kingdom,

q.prompt: Whom does the poem set out to praise?

lines.t: meotodes meahte ond his mōdgeþanc,
lines.en: the Measurer's might and his purpose,

lines.t: weorc wuldorfæder, swā hē wundra gehwæs,
lines.en: the work of the Father of glory, as he, of every wonder,

lines.t: ēce drihten, ōr onstealde!
lines.en: the eternal Lord, established the beginning.

q.prompt: What did the eternal Lord establish?

lines.t: Hē ǣrest sceōp eorðan bearnum
lines.en: He first shaped for the children of earth

lines.t: heofon tō hrōfe, hālig scyppend;
lines.en: heaven as a roof, the holy Creator;

q.prompt: What did God make first, according to the poem?

lines.t: þā middangeard, moncynnes weard,
lines.en: then the middle-earth, the guardian of mankind,

lines.t: ēce drihten, æfter tēode
lines.en: the eternal Lord, afterwards made

lines.t: fīrum foldan, frēa ælmihtig.
lines.en: the earth for men, the Lord almighty.

q.prompt: For whom was the earth made?

title: Ōhthere sǣde his hlāforde
source: The voyage of Ohthere, Old English Orosius (Lauderdale MS, text and macrons as in Bright's Anglo-Saxon Reader; trimmed)
about: Around 890 a Norwegian named Ohthere visited King Alfred and described his homeland in the far north. Alfred's scholars wrote his account into their English version of Orosius's world history. The Finnas are the Sámi.

badge.name: Northernmost
badge.about: Read Ohthere's report to King Alfred

lines.t: Ōhthere sǣde his hlāforde, Ælfrēde cyninge,
lines.en: Ohthere told his lord, King Alfred,

q.prompt: Who is Ohthere talking to?

lines.t: ðæt hē ealra Norðmonna norþmest būde.
lines.en: that he lived furthest north of all the Norwegians.

lines.t: Hē cwæð þæt hē būde on þǣm lande norþweardum wiþ þā Westsǣ.
lines.en: He said that he lived in the north of the land, along the West Sea.

q.prompt: Where did Ohthere live?
options: in the north, by the western sea
on an island in the east

lines.t: Hē sǣde þēah þæt þæt land sīe swīþe lang norþ þonan;
lines.en: He said, though, that the land runs a very long way north from there;

lines.t: ac hit is eal wēste, būton on fēawum stōwum styccemǣlum wīciað Finnas,
lines.en: but it is all wilderness, except that in a few places here and there Finnas camp,

q.prompt: Who lives in the empty land?
options: a few Finnas, here and there

lines.t: on huntoðe on wintra, ond on sumera on fiscaþe be þǣre sǣ.
lines.en: hunting in winter, and in summer fishing by the sea.

lines.t: Hē sǣde þæt hē æt sumum cirre wolde fandian
lines.en: He said that once he wanted to find out

lines.t: hū longe þæt land norþryhte lǣge.
lines.en: how far the land stretched due north.

q.prompt: What did Ohthere want to find out?
options: how far north the land went

lines.t: Þā fōr hē norþryhte be þǣm lande.
lines.en: Then he sailed due north along the land.

lines.t: Þā wæs hē swā feor norþ swā þā hwælhuntan firrest faraþ.
lines.en: Then he was as far north as the whale-hunters go at their furthest.

q.prompt: How far north had he come?
options: as far as the whale-hunters ever go
to the edge of the world

title: Ān spearwa
source: Old English Bede, the conversion of King Edwin (Latin Historia ecclesiastica II.13; Tanner MS, text and macrons as in Bright's Anglo-Saxon Reader; trimmed)
about: In 627 King Edwin of Northumbria asked his council whether to accept Christianity. One adviser answered with the picture of a sparrow flying through the king's hall in winter. This is the late ninth-century English translation of Bede's account.

badge.name: Sparrow's Flight
badge.about: Read the sparrow in the hall from the Old English Bede

lines.t: Þyslīc mē is gesewen, þū cyning, þis andwearde līf manna on eorðan,
lines.en: This is how the present life of men on earth seems to me, O king,

q.prompt: What is the adviser describing?
options: the life of men on earth

lines.t: swylc swā þū æt swǣsendum sitte
lines.en: as if you were sitting at a feast

lines.t: mid þīnum ealdormannum ond þegnum on wintertīde,
lines.en: with your noblemen and thanes in wintertime,

lines.t: ond sīe fȳr onǣlæd ond þīn heall gewyrmed,
lines.en: and the fire were lit and your hall warmed,

lines.t: cume ān spearwa ond hrædlīce þæt hūs þurhflēo,
lines.en: and a sparrow came and flew swiftly through the house,

lines.t: cume þurh ōþre duru in, þurh ōþre ūt gewīte.
lines.en: coming in through one door and going out through the other.

q.prompt: How does the sparrow pass through the hall?
options: in through one door and out through the other
down the smoke-hole and up again

lines.t: ac þæt bið ān ēagan bryhtm ond þæt lǣsste fæc,
lines.en: but that is only the blink of an eye, the shortest moment,

q.prompt: How long is the sparrow inside?
options: only the blink of an eye

lines.t: ac hē sōna of wintra on þone winter eft cymeð.
lines.en: and soon it passes out of winter into the winter again.

lines.t: Swā þonne þis monna līf tō medmiclum fæce ætȳweð;
lines.en: So this life of men appears for a little while;

q.prompt: What does the sparrow stand for?

lines.t: hwæt þǣr foregange, oððe hwæt þǣr æfterfylige, wē ne cunnun.
lines.en: what went before it, or what will follow, we do not know.

q.prompt: What does the adviser say we cannot know?
options: what comes before and after this life
how to keep a hall warm

title: Oft him ānhaga
source: The Wanderer 1–11, Exeter Book (text of ASPR III, ed. Krapp and Dobbie; macrons added)
about: The Wanderer is spoken by a warrior who has lost his lord and his companions and now crosses the winter sea alone. A narrator opens the poem, and then the wanderer begins to speak.

badge.name: Earth-Stepper
badge.about: Read the opening of The Wanderer

lines.t: Oft him ānhaga āre gebīdeð, metudes miltse,
lines.en: Often the solitary man waits for grace, for the mercy of the Measurer,

q.prompt: What does the lonely man hope for?

lines.t: þēah þe hē mōdcearig geond lagulāde longe sceolde
lines.en: though, sorrowful at heart, he has long had to, across the sea-ways,

lines.t: hrēran mid hondum hrīmcealde sǣ,
lines.en: stir the frost-cold sea with his hands,

q.prompt: What has the man been doing?

lines.t: wadan wræclāstas.
lines.en: and tread the paths of exile.

lines.t: Wyrd bið ful ārǣd!
lines.en: Fate is wholly fixed!

q.prompt: What does the poet say about fate?
options: it is fixed and cannot be changed

lines.t: Swā cwæð eardstapa, earfeþa gemyndig, wrāþra wælsleahta, winemǣga hryre:
lines.en: So spoke the earth-stepper, mindful of hardships, of cruel slaughters, of the fall of dear kinsmen:

q.prompt: What does the wanderer remember?
options: hardship, slaughter and the death of his kin

lines.t: Oft ic sceolde āna ūhtna gehwylce mīne ceare cwīþan.
lines.en: Often, alone, I have had to lament my sorrow at every dawn.

lines.t: Nis nū cwicra nān
lines.en: There is no one now among the living

lines.t: þe ic him mōdsefan mīnne durre sweotule āsecgan.
lines.en: to whom I dare speak my heart openly.

q.prompt: Why does the wanderer grieve alone?
options: no one is left he dares to open his heart to
he has sworn a vow of silence
